chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
title: Staying in the section: Chu Berry versus Ben Webster
summary: McRae argues a soloist should keep playing his part up to his solo, as Ben Webster did, unlike Chu Berry.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young

But, if you got -- you're playing eight bars -- you got eight-bar solo coming up but you're you've broadcasting and the still playing with the reed section and (inaudible) mike is right up there in front of you.
They got a mike right there for a couple of reeds and brass. But don't sit over there and leave out four bars or five bars getting ready to play your solo coming into that.
You play right up -- you going right into your solo.
That's why I always said that Ben Webster was one of the best section man there, you know, with Duke.
He always made Duke's band sound good. Well because you never missed that tenor part, although he's gonna play it -- come up with his solo. But he never left nothing off the sheet.
He played right -- kept that whole reed section together leading right into his solo.

A lot of saxophone players, they lay out two or three bars, getting themself ready to go up and play a solo. But not with Ben.

That reed section was airtight when -- That was one of the best bands that Duke had when Ben Webster was sitting in that reed section. Everybody always loved Duke when Ben was there. He was so powerful, so great for that reed section.
